title: The language and safety of chemistry
summary: Learn the fields of chemistry, symbols, formulas and the rules for working safely.
cards.0.p: Chemistry studies the structure, properties and changes of matter. Its branches are analytical, inorganic, organic, physical, bio-, polymer and industrial chemistry.
cards.0.once.soru: A chemist measures how much of each substance a medicine contains. Which branch is this?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Analytical chemistry finds which substances are in a sample and in what amounts.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Polymer chemistry studies long-chain substances such as plastics.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Industrial chemistry deals with large-scale production. Measuring what a substance contains is the job of analytical chemistry.
cards.1.p: A chemical engineer designs processes in a plant, a metallurgical engineer works with metals, and a pharmacist prepares medicines and advises on doses. Medicine, food, paint and cosmetics all depend on chemistry.
cards.1.once.soru: Who explains to a patient how and how much of a medicine to take?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: A pharmacist prepares the medicine and explains its dose and use.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: A chemical engineer designs production processes and does not give medicine to patients.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: A metallurgical engineer works with metals and alloys.
cards.2.p: In a symbol the first letter is a capital and the second is lowercase (C, Ca, Co). Some symbols come from the element's Latin name. For example, the symbol for iron is Fe, for gold Au and for lead Pb. Berzelius proposed this system in 1813.
cards.2.key: Co is cobalt, but CO is the compound carbon monoxide.
cards.3.p: A compound forms when different elements combine in a fixed ratio, and it is shown by a formula. The subscript at the lower right of a symbol tells how many of that atom there are. A subscript of 1 is not written.
cards.4.p: Besides systematic names such as sodium chloride for NaCl, compounds also have common names. For example, CaCO₃ is called limestone, HCl muriatic acid, HNO₃ aqua fortis, H₂SO₄ oil of vitriol, and NaOH caustic soda.
cards.4.etk.soru: Match each common name with the correct formula.
cards.5.h: Common names from kitchen to cleaning
cards.5.p: Some compounds are used in cooking and cleaning. They are baking soda NaHCO₃, washing soda Na₂CO₃, caustic potash KOH, ammonia NH₃, blue vitriol CuSO₄·5H₂O and bleach NaOCl. The sodas are weak bases, and the caustics are strong bases.
cards.5.svg#21: Soda: weak base · Caustic: strong base
cards.5.key: Never mix bleach with muriatic acid or ammonia, because a toxic gas is released.
cards.5.once.soru: Which one goes into the batter to make a cake rise?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Baking soda (NaHCO₃) gives off CO₂ gas when heated. These bubbles make the cake rise.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: Caustic soda (NaOH) is a strong base and burns skin. It never goes into food.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Blue vitriol (copper sulfate) is toxic and used in farming. It never goes into food.
cards.6.p: Symbols with a red border describe a hazard. A flame means flammable, an exploding bomb means explosive, and a flame over a circle means oxidizing. A skull means toxic, and an exclamation mark means irritant. The corrosive symbol shows liquid dripping onto a hand.
cards.6.svg#6: Others: compressed gas, serious health hazard, harmful to the environment
cards.6.key: Recognizing the symbol is the first thing to do before you open a bottle.
cards.7.p: In the lab you wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves. Acid is always added to water. Chemicals are never smelled or tasted. You do not eat in the lab, you do not pour waste down the sink, and you do not use unlabeled bottles.
cards.7.svg#0: Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves
cards.7.svg#1: Add acid to water, not water to acid
cards.7.svg#2: Do not smell or taste chemicals
cards.7.svg#3: Do not eat or drink in the lab
cards.7.svg#4: Do not pour waste down the sink
cards.7.key: If a chemical splashes into your eye, rinse with plenty of water for at least 15 minutes and report it right away.
cards.8.p: The body needs some elements. Calcium works in bones, iron in hemoglobin, and sodium and potassium in nerve signals. Heavy metals such as mercury, lead and cadmium build up in the body and cause harm.
cards.8.once.soru: Which element is in hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: The iron in hemoglobin binds oxygen. Iron deficiency causes anemia.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Lead is a heavy metal that builds up in the body and causes harm.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Mercury is toxic and has no job in the body.
cards.9.p:
• Chemistry has branches and is used in many careers.
• In a symbol the first letter is a capital and the second is lowercase. The subscript in a formula shows the number of atoms.
• Compounds also have common names.
• Know the hazard symbols and follow the lab rules.
• Some elements are essential for the body, while heavy metals are harmful.
quiz.0.q: Match each substance with the hazard symbol you should see on its bottle.
quiz.0.e: Kerosene catches fire easily. Potassium nitrate gives off oxygen and makes burning more intense. Cyanide kills even in tiny amounts. Concentrated sulfuric acid eats away skin and metal.
quiz.1.q: Put each element in the right group.
quiz.1.e: Calcium works in bones and teeth, iron in hemoglobin, and sodium and potassium in nerve signals. Mercury, lead and cadmium build up in the body and damage organs.
quiz.2.q: How many atoms in total are in one H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> molecule?
quiz.2.e: Subscripts show the number of atoms. 2 H + 1 S + 4 O = 7 atoms. The subscript of S is 1, so it is not written.
quiz.3.q: What is the right way to dilute an acid?
quiz.3.o.0: Add the acid slowly to water
quiz.3.o.1: Pour water quickly onto the acid
quiz.3.o.2: Pour both into the container at once
quiz.3.o.3: Heat the acid, then add water
quiz.3.e: Acid is added slowly to water. If water is poured onto acid, the heat released boils the water and can splash the acid.
quiz.3.y.1: The first drops of water poured onto acid boil from the heat released and splash the acid. That is why acid is added slowly to water.
quiz.3.y.2: Pouring both at once does not stop the heat from being released out of control. Acid should be added to water a little at a time.
quiz.3.y.3: Heating the acid makes it more dangerous. Heat is released during dilution, so acid is added slowly to cold water.
A:baslik: The language and safety of chemistry
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Build formulas, decode symbols and recognize hazard symbols.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Add atoms to build water, H₂O.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: Two hydrogens and one oxygen combine to form H₂O. The subscript of oxygen is 1, so it is not written. The water molecule is bent, not straight.
A:adimlar.1.metin: This molecule is CO, carbon monoxide, a toxic gas. Add one more oxygen to make the CO₂ you breathe out.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: CO₂ is called carbon dioxide. A single oxygen completely changes the substance. CO sticks to the hemoglobin in blood and blocks oxygen transport. CO₂ is already in the air you breathe.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Some symbols come from the element's Latin name. For example, the symbol for iron is Fe (ferrum) and for gold Au (aurum). Decode this symbol.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: Sn is the symbol for which element?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Sn comes from stannum, the Latin name for tin. A food can is steel with a thin coating of tin.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The symbol for sodium is Na, from its Latin name natrium.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The symbol for silicon is Si. Sn comes from the Latin name stannum.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: NaCl is called sodium chloride, which is table salt. Salt is actually a crystal made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. The formula shows their 1 to 1 ratio.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Look at the symbol on the label before you open the bottle.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The flame symbol marks flammable substances such as alcohol, acetone and gasoline. They are kept away from flames and sparks.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The explosive symbol shows an exploding bomb.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: A toxic substance is marked with a skull.
A:adimlar.5.metin: This symbol looks like the first one, but there is a circle under the flame. This small difference means a very different hazard.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Which kind of substance does this symbol mark?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The flame over a circle marks substances that do not burn themselves but give off oxygen and start or intensify burning. Concentrated hydrogen peroxide is an example. These are kept away from flammable substances.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The flammable symbol shows only a flame, with no circle under it.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The corrosive symbol shows liquid dripping onto a hand and a surface and eating them away.
A:adimlar.6.metin: You need to dilute a concentrated acid. A lot of heat is released when acid and water mix.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: Add the acid slowly to water
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: When acid is added a little at a time to plenty of water, the heat spreads through the large mass of water and nothing splashes. That is why acid is always added to water.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A little water on top of the acid heats up suddenly, boils and splashes the acid.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: It does matter, because if water is added to acid, the hot water can splash the acid.
A:kapanis.0: In a symbol the first letter is a capital and the second is lowercase. Co is cobalt, while CO is carbon monoxide.
A:kapanis.1: The subscript in a formula shows how many of that atom there are. A subscript of 1 is not written (H₂O, CO₂).
A:kapanis.2: Some symbols come from Latin names. Fe comes from ferrum, Au from aurum and Pb from plumbum.
A:kapanis.3: Diamond-shaped symbols with a red border describe hazards. A flame marks a flammable substance, and a flame over a circle marks an oxidizing substance.
A:kapanis.4: When diluting, add acid to water slowly, never the other way around.
